I am 65 years old and have farmed these lands in Quzhou for 40 years. I know every corner of my 10.1 mu. My household has six people, but my son and daughter-in-law work in a factory in Handan, so they only come back during busy seasons. That means the day-to-day work falls mainly on me, my wife, and my younger daughter. I finished middle school, so I understand what the extension agent says, but I still trust my own eyes and what Old Zhang down the road does more than any leaflet.

It is the start of the season now. The wheat I planted last October is greening up, and I am already thinking about the jointing topdressing in March. I keep 6.5 mu in the wheat-maize double cropping system — that is my backbone. Wheat gives us grain security, and maize brings steady cash. I only plant 3.6 mu of cotton. Cotton can pay well when prices are good, but at my age, crawling through the fields for picking in autumn is hard on my back, and with my son away I cannot rely on hired labor for everything. This split gives me income diversification without killing myself.

For the wheat, I bought an improved variety from the county supply store. I learned my lesson years ago when I tried cheap seed from the market — the yield was terrible. I rotary till after the maize comes off in October, broadcast seed and fertilizer, then drag a plank to cover. I put down about 16 kg of nitrogen per mu in total — a compound fertilizer base before planting, and then at jointing I topdress with urea if the wheat looks a bit yellow. The extension man says 15 kg is enough, but I would rather waste a little money than risk a bad year. I irrigate three times from my well: once before winter to help the seedlings establish, once at jointing in March, and once during grain filling in May. The electricity bill adds up, but you cannot skip water if you want good wheat.

For summer maize, the turnaround after wheat harvest is brutally tight — sometimes only two or three days. I use hybrid seed, and I plant with a no-tillage hand planter to save time. All the fertilizer goes in the furrow at planting because there is no time for split application. I irrigate twice: once right after planting if the soil is dry, and once at tasseling. The summer rains usually help, so two times is enough if the season is normal.

For cotton, I plough the 3.6 mu deeply in early April because cotton likes loose soil. I use an improved variety. I put down compound fertilizer as a base and topdress once during flowering. I irrigate twice and spray pesticides four times because aphids and bollworm are always lurking. My family will pick the early bolls together in autumn, and if we fall behind, I will ask my son to take a few days off.

I expect about 450 kg per mu from the wheat, 500 kg per mu from the maize, and 260 kg per mu of lint from the cotton. These targets are conservative but achievable — about what I got last year and what my successful neighbors typically harvest. At my age, I am not chasing records. I want steady income, enough to cover my grandson's school fees, and a bit left over for my wife and me.
